title: Poll Studio: stable options and reliable edits
focus: identity in dynamic arrays and commit-before-publish
before: Vote preservation depended on option count and position. Removing a row could reset other votes, and a failed write could leave memory ahead of storage.
after: Draft options carry stable ids. Surviving options retain their votes; new options start at zero. Blank or duplicate labels are rejected. Save, vote, reset and delete publish state only after storage succeeds.
model: A poll has id, question and options. An option has its own id, text and votes. Drafts contain id/text; they become the saved poll only at commit. Data lives under js1-poll-studio in localStorage.
concept:
An index describes position, not identity. If A, B and C have 4, 7 and 2 votes, deleting A moves B from index 1 to 0. Matching by position can now attach the wrong votes. Matching by id finds the same option wherever it appears. A new option receives a fresh id, so it cannot inherit removed votes. Renaming an existing option preserves its votes; the app treats that as a label correction, not a new election choice.

Validation precedes candidate construction. Trimming labels is normalization; rejecting equal case-folded labels is validation. A storage quota failure leaves the saved poll and current draft available for retry. The candidate does not become authoritative until setItem succeeds. This is a local poll builder, not a secure voting system.
example: Remove Mobile app from the starter poll. Public API retains 7 votes and Dark mode retains 2, for 9 total. Duplicate labels API/api are rejected. A failed write preserves both the old poll and the current draft.
exercises: Reorder option rows without detaching their votes.
Distinguish correcting a label from replacing its meaning.
Add a confirmation before resetting votes.
Validate a full imported poll graph.
answers: Move complete draft objects, including ids; assert votes still match ids after submit.
Correction keeps the id. Explicit replacement should allocate a new id and start at zero, with clear wording.
Build the zero-vote candidate only after confirmation. Cancel must not change storage or state.
Check unique ids, bounded strings, 2-6 options and nonnegative safe-integer votes. Reject malformed imports as a whole.

title: Kanban Flow: keyboard moves and saved order
focus: immutable movement, ordering invariants and keyboard access
before: Dragging changed a live card before saving, renumbered only the destination, and made self-drops surprising. Movement required drag events.
after: Moves validate targets, ignore self-drops, calculate a candidate and renumber every column before saving. Failed moves preserve state. Column selects and move-up/down buttons support keyboard use and restore focus.
model: Each card has id, title, column and order. Column is todo/doing/done; order is a zero-based position within that column. The browser stores the card array under js1-kanban-flow.
concept:
A move changes both membership and sibling order. Moving A out of [A,B] should leave B at order 0. Inserting A before C elsewhere should yield A=0 and C=1. Cloning first makes the intended result reviewable without mutating the current board.

A re-render replaces DOM elements, so focus can disappear even when a keyboard button works. Restoring focus to the moved card lets the user continue without returning to the top. The select expresses destination; up/down expresses order. Both paths call the same move function so keyboard and drag behavior cannot drift apart. Other legacy CRUD paths are outside the failed-move guarantee.
example: Move A from todo [A,B] before C in doing. B becomes order 0; A/C become orders 0/1. A self-drop does nothing. Reject setItem and the previous card array remains identical.
exercises: Disable up/down at column boundaries.
Add a drag insertion marker.
Enforce a doing-column work-in-progress limit.
Replace prompt-based renaming with an inline form.
answers: Derive boundary state from cardsIn, while retaining handler guards.
Show the intended beforeId without changing storage until drop.
Count destination cards excluding the moved id; enforce the rule in moveCard for both input methods.
Use a candidate title update, persist first and retain the form on failure.

title: Course Roster: unique codes and capacity
focus: normalization, uniqueness and whole-number invariants
before: NaN and fractional counts could evade simple comparisons, and equivalent course codes could be created twice.
after: Codes and text are bounded and typed. Capacity/enrollment must be whole counts, enrollment cannot exceed capacity, levels are constrained, and normalized codes are unique across other records. Editing can retain its own code.
model: Courses contain id, uppercase code, title, instructor, capacity, enrolled and level. Available seats is capacity minus enrolled. Records are in server memory and reset on restart.
concept:
Number("bad") yields NaN, whose lower-bound comparisons are false. Check representation and Number.isSafeInteger before applying capacity rules. Only then is enrolled <= capacity meaningful.

Uniqueness must use consistent normalization. Trim and uppercase the candidate before comparing codes. Exclude the edited id, or an unchanged code conflicts with itself. The array scan is appropriate for one process; a database version needs a uniqueness constraint because separate processes can otherwise both pass a preflight check. A controlled form assists users, but the API must validate direct requests too.
example: Create astra-101 with capacity 4 and enrolled 2: the returned code is ASTRA-101. A second equivalent code returns 409. Editing the original title succeeds. Capacity 1.5, enrollment 5 or null is rejected.
exercises: Add an enroll-one command.
Show a derived full-course badge.
Move uniqueness into a database.
Preview capacity reductions.
answers: Compute from the current course and validate before publishing; do not accept an arbitrary replacement record.
Use enrolled === capacity rather than storing a second mutable flag.
Normalize before saving and enforce a unique normalized code in SQL; test competing inserts.
Display proposed capacity minus enrollment and reject a negative result rather than deleting enrollments.

title: Event Admin: real dates and registration limits
focus: calendar labels and cross-field validation
before: Dates were checked only for presence. NaN and fractional registration counts could pass comparisons.
after: Events require bounded text, real YYYY-MM-DD dates and whole capacity/registration counts. Registered cannot exceed capacity. Invalid updates preserve the previous event.
model: Event fields are id, name, location, date, capacity, registered and status. A calendar date is not an instant. Availability is derived; records remain in memory.
concept:
A regular expression recognizes the shape of 2027-02-29 but cannot decide if it exists. Parse a UTC reference date and compare the result with the original label; rollover exposes invalid days. UTC validates the label without assigning a time to the event.

Validate each count before relating them. A full event is valid, so equality must pass; one registration beyond capacity must fail. Missing, null, fractional and nonnumeric values deserve separate fixtures because JavaScript conversions can make them look deceptively similar. Rejection must happen before replacing the original record.
example: 2028-02-29 with capacity 3 and registered 3 succeeds. 2027-02-29, 2028-04-31, registered 4 and capacity "bad" fail without replacing a saved event.
exercises: Add register-one.
Model a waitlist separately.
Sort events chronologically.
Extend the model to timed events.
answers: Compute and validate a candidate; a database version needs a conditional update or transaction.
Keep confirmed and waiting counts distinct; promotion changes both together.
Compare valid YYYY-MM-DD strings, then id for same-day ties.
Define a timezone and instant representation explicitly rather than appending an arbitrary Z.

title: Job Pipeline: follow-up dates and ordering
focus: optional values and stable chronological sorting
before: Follow-up dates were not validated and matching applications followed insertion order.
after: Text fields are bounded and typed. Nonempty next-step dates must be real dates. Filtered results sort by date, place undated applications last, and use ids for ties.
model: Applications contain id, company, role, stage, contact, nextStepDate and notes. Empty nextStepDate means unscheduled. Stage and search filter an in-memory collection.
concept:
Empty and invalid are different. Leaving a follow-up unscheduled is intentional; February 30 is malformed. Preserve the empty-string convention while rejecting invalid nonempty labels.

Undated applications should not acquire invented urgency. The comparison places their sentinel after valid dates, then uses id for stable ties. Sorting the filtered copy preserves the underlying collection. This is chronological display ordering, not a reminder service: it sends no notifications and changes no workflow stages automatically. A rejected edit must leave the saved application intact.
example: Dates March 10, March 1 and empty display as March 1, March 10, empty. An invalid follow-up edit returns 400 and leaves the original application identical.
exercises: Add an overdue filter with an injected today.
Record follow-up completion.
Offer company sorting.
Test changing a date to empty.
answers: Compare only valid nonempty labels and supply today explicitly in tests.
Separate completion history from scheduling the next date; define their atomic boundary.
Whitelist sort choices and use normalized company plus id.
Preserve id and verify the application moves after dated matches.

title: Stock Catalog: stable pages and numeric inputs
focus: filter-sort-slice order and numeric boundaries
before: Fractional/infinite paging values were insufficiently normalized, sort ties lacked a unique tie-breaker and malformed prices reached unsafe paths.
after: Paging normalizes to bounded whole values. Sort ties use ids. Names/categories are bounded text, prices are finite and bounded, and stock is a nonnegative whole count. Existing last-page clamping has regression coverage.
model: Products have id, name, category, price and stock. The API returns items and page metadata. The client holds one page; the repository itself remains in memory.
concept:
Filter, then sort, then slice. Slicing first produces sparse pages and misleading totals. Equal prices still need a unique tie-breaker to make boundaries deterministic.

Requested and returned pages can differ after deletion. The server knows the filtered total and clamps to its last real page; the client should display that metadata. Infinity is not a valid price just because it is >= 0. Checking finite values, whole stock counts and accepted text representations prevents conversions from hiding malformed input. Pagination does not add persistence or concurrency guarantees to an in-memory store.
example: Three same-price products at two per page give stable ids on page 1. Page 999 becomes page 2 with one item. Infinite/fractional page inputs use defaults; infinite prices and fractional stock are rejected.
exercises: Add filtered inventory value across all pages.
Add a secondary sort choice.
Translate paging into SQL.
Delete the final row of the final page.
answers: Aggregate before slicing; visible-page value is a different metric.
Whitelist both keys and retain id as the final tie-breaker.
Bind filters and whitelist ORDER BY identifiers; keep count and rows consistent.
Refetch and verify clamping with the correct total rather than showing an empty phantom page.

title: Recipe Studio: nested ingredient validation
focus: array element validation and normalization
before: NaN cooking values could evade checks, ingredient objects were coerced into text, and repeated labels were duplicated.
after: Cooking minutes and servings are bounded whole numbers. Ingredients must be 1-100 nonempty bounded strings. Trimming and case-insensitive deduplication preserve first spelling. Invalid nested payloads are rejected before mutation.

concept:
Checking Array.isArray is only the first step: an array can hold objects, null or blank strings. Validate each element before building the normalized recipe. String(object) hides malformed input as [object Object].

Use one representation for comparison and another for display. Salt and salt compare equal, while the first trimmed spelling stays visible. Do not infer that "1 tsp salt" equals "salt"; this app lacks a structured quantity model. Automatic scaling would require that model first. The focused regression suite demonstrates valid normalization and rejected nested values.

Add a scale preview.
Explain when deduplication is wrong.
Add ingredient reordering.

Salt for a sauce and a topping may be separate; model sections before collapsing them.

title: Org Explorer: keeping a tree acyclic
focus: recursive queries, structural invariants and concurrent tree moves
before: The ancestor check and move were separate operations. Two simultaneous moves could each see an acceptable old tree and together create a cycle.
after: Moves validate UUIDs and parent existence, lock structural changes within a transaction, check the subtree under the lock, then update. A node cannot become its own ancestor.
model: Each node has a UUID, name, title and nullable parent_id. A null parent means a root. Children point upward; recursive SQL discovers descendants. A valid forest may have several roots, but every parent chain must terminate.
concept:
Consider two roots A and B. Request one proposes A under B; request two proposes B under A. Both are valid against the initial tree. Checking first and updating later leaves a time-of-check/time-of-use gap. The transaction takes a SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE table lock before validating the structure. The second writer waits, then sees the first committed move and rejects the cycle. A transaction alone at the default isolation level would not make two independent read-then-write checks safe.

The lock is deliberately broad: it serializes structural writers for this small teaching app. It is easy to explain and inspect, but reduces concurrent write throughput. A more scalable design requires a proven locking or serializable-retry strategy, not simply removing the lock. The API policy cannot prevent arbitrary direct SQL from creating a cycle if that SQL bypasses the validation. The recursive query and the lock solve different parts of the problem: reachability and concurrency.
example: Create roots A and B. Race A-under-B with B-under-A. Exactly one succeeds; the rejected move leaves a readable acyclic tree. Moving A under its own descendant is rejected even without concurrency.
exercises: Show the full ancestor breadcrumb for a selected node.
Add a dry-run move endpoint that explains rejection.
Exercise three concurrent structural moves.
Design a more concurrent alternative to the table lock.
answers: Walk parent ids with a visited set and show names from root to leaf; missing parents should produce an explicit diagnostic.
Reuse validation, but explain that a dry run is advisory because the tree can change before the real move. The actual move must revalidate under its lock.
Use separate requests/connections and assert the final parent graph terminates from every node, rather than assuming a particular winner.
Compare serializable transactions with retry against a carefully ordered lock set. Write the conflicting schedule and prove it cannot commit a cycle before implementing.

title: Pulse Analytics: truthful daily charts
focus: calendar buckets, window functions and derived data
before: A chart based only on existing event dates omitted quiet days, so a seven-row average could cover more than seven calendar days.
after: The series generates every requested calendar day, left-joins daily aggregates, fills missing values with zero and computes the moving average and cumulative total over those rows. Summary uses the same inclusive day window.
model: Raw events are timestamped facts with event type, product and purchase amount. Daily aggregates and materialized views are derived data. The chart returns one row per calendar date; a missing event row becomes a zero-valued day rather than disappearing.
concept:
SQL GROUP BY only produces groups present in the input. If Monday has 10 purchases and Wednesday has 20, Tuesday does not exist in the grouped result. generate_series supplies the calendar spine. LEFT JOIN keeps Tuesday, and COALESCE converts the missing aggregate to zero. Only then does a ROWS window correspond to calendar days. The order of these operations is part of correctness.

The first moving-average points use the available rows inside the requested window; the first point is a one-day average, not a hidden seven-day warm-up. Cumulative totals also reset at the requested window boundary, and the first delta is null because there is no preceding row in that result. Summary and series share inclusive calendar-day boundaries. The separate top-products query retains a rolling timestamp window. Refreshing a materialized view is an explicit update to a stored derived result; newly inserted raw events can exist before that view reflects them.
example: For daily values 10, 0 and 20, the visible moving averages are 10, 5 and 10; cumulative totals are 10, 10 and 30. A seven-day request returns seven rows even if events exist on only two days.
exercises: Add a tooltip that distinguishes zero activity from loading.
Compare an average with and without zero days.
Add an explicit materialized-view freshness indicator.
Offer an optional moving-average warm-up period.
answers: Use request state for loading and a numeric zero for a completed empty day. Do not use a falsy check that hides zero.

title: Support Tickets: repeat-safe workflow history
focus: row locks, atomic updates and meaningful audit events
before: Repeated status or assignment requests could append duplicate history even when the requested value already matched the ticket.
after: Status and assignment read the current ticket under a row lock, return it unchanged for a repeated value, and record actual changes transactionally. Input and UUID validation reject malformed requests; failed related writes roll back.
model: Tickets reference agents and labels. A ticket has current status and optional assigned agent; history explains actual changes. Junction rows connect tickets to labels. These separate rows must remain consistent with the ticket operation that creates them.
concept:
An audit event should describe a transition, not merely a button click. With status Open, requesting Resolved twice should produce one Open-to-Resolved event. Both requests must compare against the current locked row. Otherwise two concurrent callers can each read Open and both log the same transition. SELECT FOR UPDATE makes the second caller wait and inspect the committed value.

The same idea applies to assignment, including assigning the same agent twice. The update and corresponding event belong in the same transaction and use the same database client. Throwing after one successful query does not undo that query unless it is inside a transaction that rolls back. Foreign keys protect references, but a malformed UUID should be rejected before it becomes an opaque database error. This is repeat-safe current-state handling, not global request deduplication: if another valid transition happens between two commands, the later command may create a new event.
example: Create a ticket, resolve it twice, and read history. There is one status event. Repeat assigning the same agent with the same expectation. Force a late related write to fail and verify that the earlier ticket changes did not commit.

Suppose six matching threads use a five-row page. Page two has one item. Deleting it leaves five matches, so page two no longer exists. title: Asset Checkout: reliable workflow and history
focus: atomic status transitions, consistent pages and calendar dates
before: Status requests could add redundant history. Validation accepted malformed shapes, and page calculations lacked a consistent clamped result. Separate status and history writes could disagree after a late failure; separate count/page queries could see different snapshots. Seed dueDate values also needed correct JSON-to-SQL field mapping.
after: Typed and bounded inputs protect edits, real calendar dates round-trip, page numbers clamp and equal sort values use an id tie-breaker. Repeating the current status creates no extra status history. Status and audit writes use one row-locked transaction; count and rows share a repeatable-read snapshot. Seed dates map to the intended column. The shared toolbar now uses two flexible columns so its search field remains readable beside the form and activity panels.
model: This app represents an equipment checkout and its custodian. A record uses generic fields id, title, owner, category, status, priority, amount, dueDate and notes. Categories are Laptop, Camera, Tooling, Vehicle. Statuses are Available, Checked Out, Maintenance, Retired. The UI gives these shared fields domain-specific labels. Return date is represented as a YYYY-MM-DD calendar string, not an instant. PostgreSQL items and activity_entries tables persist records and their child history.
concept:
Follow one concrete command: change "Camera kit for field interviews" from Available to Checked Out. The first successful command represents a real transition and adds one status event. Sending Checked Out again compares equal to current state, so it returns the record without adding another status event. Created, updated and note entries remain separate kinds; counting every timeline row would give the wrong assertion. This guarantee concerns repeated current values, not global request deduplication. After an intervening transition, requesting Checked Out can legitimately create a new event.

The handler obtains one database client, begins a transaction and reads the record FOR UPDATE. A second writer waits for that row, then compares against its latest committed status. The update and activity insert use the same client, so an audit-insert failure rolls back the status too. The test installs a temporary trigger to force that late failure. Separately, the list transaction counts and fetches under one repeatable-read snapshot. It does not freeze the dataset across later HTTP requests. PostgreSQL DATE values are returned as calendar strings through a type parser, avoiding accidental local-midnight conversion.

Validation belongs at the API boundary even when the React controls constrain input. An object is not a valid title, an unknown priority is not silently accepted, and 2027-02-29 is not a real date. Normalization may trim a valid string, but should not stringify an object into a misleading title. For paging, count matching rows before clamping a request such as page 999. Sort by the selected field and then id so ties are deterministic on an unchanged dataset. The scaffold accepts its named statuses; it does not enforce a domain approval graph or actor permissions. Add a UI confirmation for changing Checked Out back to Available.
Add a regression for a return date at a leap-year boundary.
Prevent checking out an already checked-out asset
